transcript.content: Hello, how are you doing today? What brings you in to see me?

I’m… well, I’m here because I think I’ve let this go on too long, honestly. The thing that finally pushed me to make the appointment is how tense my body has become. My neck and shoulders are tight almost all the time now, and even my jaw — I catch myself clenching it without realizing.

It’s not just after a long day teaching or carrying books around or anything like that. It’s when I’m sitting at my desk, or even at home trying to watch TV in the evening. I’ll suddenly notice I’m sort of braced, like I’m waiting for bad news or preparing for something to go wrong, even when nothing is happening. It’s become hard to ignore.
Do you find yourself worrying a lot about different things — maybe work, relationships, or other responsibilities — even when there isn’t a clear reason to be concerned?

Yes. Very much so. It’s not even one particular thing I can point to and say, “That’s the problem.” My mind just keeps moving from one worry to the next.

Like, I’ll be thinking about the house and whether the contractors missed something, or whether I should have checked their work more carefully. Then almost immediately I’m on to school — wondering if my lesson plans are slipping, if I’m not staying on top of things the way I should. And then it’s the robotics kids, whether they’re falling behind because I haven’t guided them enough or planned enough.

And then it becomes more personal, I suppose. I start worrying that I’m disappointing my wife, or my family, because I’m not keeping everything under control the way I feel like I’m supposed to. It’s like my head is constantly scanning for something I may have neglected, even when there isn’t a clear reason to think anything is actually wrong.
Have you ever experienced sudden episodes where you feel intense fear or discomfort that comes on quickly, maybe with symptoms like a racing heart, sweating, or shortness of breath?

I don’t think so… not in the way you’re describing, where it suddenly hits like a wave and my heart is racing or I can’t breathe or anything like that.

I mean, I do get worked up, and I can feel very on edge, but it’s more like a constant build-up or a background hum that gets louder, if that makes sense. I’m not sure I’ve had an episode where I’d say, “That was a panic attack,” or something sudden and intense out of nowhere. It’s more ongoing than sudden.
Are there times when you experience physical tension or discomfort even when you’re not thinking about work, family, or other responsibilities?

Yes, definitely. That’s actually the part that made me think, “All right, this isn’t just normal stress anymore.”

I’ll be sitting at my desk, not even actively thinking through some problem, and I’ll realize my shoulders are up near my ears, or my neck feels like it’s been locked in place for hours. And my jaw — I catch myself clenching it without even noticing I was doing it. It’s strange because sometimes I’m just watching TV at night, something completely ordinary, and my body still feels braced, like I’m waiting for bad news.

It’s almost like the tension is there before I even know what I’m supposedly worried about. That’s what’s been hard to ignore.

Have you noticed this muscle tension or physical discomfort happening specifically when you're trying to fall asleep or during the night, like clenching your jaw or tensing your muscles while you're asleep?

Yes… especially at night, I think. I mean, I notice it during the day too, but when I’m trying to settle down it becomes much harder to ignore because there’s nothing distracting me.

I’ll be sitting at my desk or even just watching TV in the evening, and my neck and shoulders are already tight, like I’m sort of holding myself rigid without realizing it. Then when I go to bed, I can feel that same tightness still there. My jaw is a big one too — I catch myself clenching it, and sometimes I only notice because my face feels tired or sore.

It’s like my body doesn’t really switch off. Even when I’m not doing anything stressful, it feels like I’m bracing for something, like waiting for bad news, and I can’t seem to get my muscles to fully let go. That’s honestly one of the things that finally made me come in, because it feels like it’s almost all the time now.
Do you find it hard to relax, even when you know logically that everything is okay or when you're not actively thinking about something stressful?

Yes, very much so. That’s actually a good way of putting it — because logically, I can tell myself, “Nothing is happening right now, the room is quiet, the day is basically over,” but my body and my mind don’t seem to take that in.

Most of the day I feel sort of wound up, like I’m waiting for the next thing to go wrong. It’s not always tied to one clear thought either. At school, between periods, I’ll catch myself pacing around the classroom instead of just sitting for a minute. I’ll straighten things on my desk, walk to the door, check the hallway, then check my phone. Lately I’ve been checking for messages from the contractor a lot, even when I know there’s probably nothing new and checking won’t make anything happen faster.

And I know that sounds small, but it’s the feeling behind it. Like I can’t just let things be still. Even when everything is technically okay, there’s this pressure in me, like I’m supposed to be preparing for something. Relaxing almost feels… unsafe, I guess, or unnatural lately.
Have you noticed feeling unusually tired or fatigued, even if you haven’t been doing anything physically demanding?

Yes, I have. That’s actually been one of the more frustrating parts, because I can’t always point to something I physically did that would explain it.

By the time the last bell rings at school, I feel completely wrung out — not just “I had a busy day” tired, but like I’ve been holding myself together all day and then suddenly there’s nothing left. And then I’ll sit down to grade what should be a short stack of quizzes, nothing major, and it feels like pushing through mud. I’ll read the same answer a few times and just feel this heaviness, like even starting takes more effort than it should.

And the annoying thing is, a decent night’s sleep doesn’t really reset it the way I’d expect. Even a quiet Sunday, where I’m not running around or doing anything demanding, doesn’t fully fix it. I might rest, but I don’t feel restored, if that makes sense. It’s more like I’m dragging this tiredness around with me.
Do you find yourself feeling restless or physically unable to sit still, like you need to keep moving or doing something even when you're not actively stressed?

Yes, definitely. I think that’s one of the things I notice most during the school day.

I feel wound up a lot of the time, almost like I’m waiting for something else to go wrong, even if nothing specific is happening in that moment. Between periods, when I technically could just sit at my desk for five minutes, I don’t. I’ll get up and pace around the classroom, straighten papers, move things that don’t really need moving, look out into the hallway, then check my phone.

The phone checking has been a big one lately because of the contractor. I’ll keep looking for messages, even though I know perfectly well that if he hasn’t replied, staring at the phone isn’t going to make him reply faster. But I still feel this urge to check, like I need to be doing something. Sitting still just feels really uncomfortable, like I’m wasting a chance to prevent some problem from happening.
Have you noticed yourself becoming more irritable or easily annoyed, even over small things that wouldn’t have bothered you before?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, everyone gets annoyed, and teaching teenagers all day can test anyone’s patience, so it’s hard for me to separate what’s just normal irritation from something unusual.

I wouldn’t say I’ve clearly noticed myself snapping at people or getting angry over tiny things in a way that feels completely out of character. There are moments where I feel a bit short, but I can usually catch it before it comes out, or at least I think I can. It’s not the main thing I’ve been aware of.

So… maybe a little here and there, but I can’t confidently say, yes, I’m much more irritable than before. That’s not something I’ve been tracking as clearly.
Have you noticed any trouble focusing or keeping your attention on tasks, like difficulty following through on what you're reading or struggling to make decisions, even small ones?

I don’t know that I can give you a clear yes on that. I mean, I have moments where I’ll reread something or take longer to settle into a task, but I’m not sure if that’s really a concentration problem or just… normal end-of-day brain fog, especially with teaching.

With reading, if it’s something dense or administrative, I might catch myself drifting a bit and have to go back over a paragraph, but I wouldn’t say I’m completely unable to follow things. And with decisions, small ones can sometimes feel more annoying than they should, like choosing what to tackle first, but I can usually make myself pick something and get on with it.

So I guess I’ve noticed little bits of that here and there, but not enough that I’d confidently say, “Yes, my focus is clearly impaired.” It’s more that I’m not sure where the line is between normal mental tiredness and something more significant.
